findings.message: The fix adds two guards in movedFrom (`olds.length !== 1` and `news.length !== 1`), but only the named case is tested: one removed folder copied to two new numbers, which hits the `news` guard. Nothing tests the `olds` side of the one-to-one pairing, so deleting `olds.length !== 1 ||` leaves every row of the table green. Add variant rows to the table: (a) two removed folders with the same slug and one new folder that matches one of them must be judged (fail); (b) a removed folder that comes back as an archived copy plus a renumbered active copy, e.g. gone('074-demo') + folder('074-demo', {archived:true}) + folder('099-demo'), must be judged.
findings.scenario: Base has 074-demo and 080-demo, both with slug 'demo'. A fork PR deletes both and adds 099-demo, identical to 074-demo apart from the name. Without the `olds` guard, `[old] = olds` picks 074-demo, 099-demo is skipped as a move, and the gate exits 0. Every test still passes, so the guard is unproven.

findings.message: Line 5 still works out the slug inline with `NUMBERED.exec(name)?.[2]`, and line 7 now defines `slugOf` to do the same thing. Define `slugOf` once and use it on line 5 too.

AC-7 still defines a move as 'the old folder is gone, the new one has the same slug, and every file matches'. It says nothing about the one-to-one pairing the code now needs: exactly one removed folder and exactly one new folder with that slug. A reader of AC-7 would expect each of two identical copies to be skipped. Amend AC-7 to state the pairing.
